strengths: The core idea is fresh and well-motivated: bypassing the generative decode-encode loop and using undecoded latents (3D and audio) directly as privileged information is a clean, practically relevant observation for LUPI-style pipelines, with quantified savings (87.7% inference time and 600 MB VRAM for 3D; 20.6% time and 23.8% VRAM for audio).

The empirical case is structured sensibly: Table 1 isolates the latent-vs-raw teacher question, Table 2 ablates modality contributions and includes modality-only training to probe generative shortcuts, and Table 3 compares against KD and LUGPI with 3 runs and standard deviations.

The MESSy analysis goes beyond accuracy: the NMI alignment study (Fig. 3) against hand-crafted and deep audio/3D feature clusters, and the class-level qualitative analysis (Fig. 4) linking acoustic vs geometric improvements to plausible classes, provide interpretability evidence for the 'emergent synesthesia' claim.

The paper is clearly written with a well-organized three-phase pipeline (Fig. 2) and a coherent narrative connecting the Data Processing Inequality argument, capacity interference, and the predictive (rather than matching) distillation objective.
The proposed approach is deployment-friendly: auxiliary heads are discarded at inference, giving a unimodal student with zero added inference cost, which matches the paper's stated motivation.
weaknesses: Scale and generality of the evaluation are limited: experiments are confined to Imagenette2-320, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100. For a paper claiming a general paradigm shift in synthetic privileged information, the absence of full ImageNet or any larger/fine-grained benchmark weakens the external validity of the claims.

The 'capacity interference' hypothesis — the central motivation for MESSy over L2 matching — is supported only indirectly by LUGPI underperforming. No direct evidence (e.g., student feature distortion measurements, hyperparameter sensitivity of the L2 baseline, or normalization/weighting controls) is provided to rule out that LUGPI simply needs tuning. Predicting teacher pooled tokens through learnable heads is essentially FitNets-style hint learning, so the distillation contribution is incremental and the comparison to that lineage could be sharper.

A potential information-leakage concern is under-addressed: audio latents are conditioned on Gemma3 captions generated from the image, and 3D latents are generated directly from image queries. The modality-only results (e.g., audio-only 54.61% on Imagenette2) suggest the synthetic modalities carry substantial class-correlated signal; the argument that this reflects 'physical priors' rather than image-derived discriminative features is plausible but not conclusively established, and the narrative of 'properties never directly observed' may be somewhat overstated.

Baselines are relatively thin on the distillation side: only KD and LUGPI are compared. Stronger cross-modal distillation methods (e.g., relational/contrastive distillation like CRD), a raw-data teacher distilled with the same MESSy objective (to disentangle DLA gains from MESSy gains for the student), and a raw-synthetic LUGPI variant are missing. Key ablations (K layers, dropout rate p=0.8) are deferred to supplementary material not visible here.

The DPI-based motivation (Sec. 3.1) is heuristic: decoding is deterministic, so I(Y;Z) >= I(Y;X̂) holds, but the claim that this translates into downstream accuracy is an empirical one, and the theoretical framing adds more rhetoric than rigor.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned, and important details (generation prompts, filtering, Perceiver configurations, training schedules) are relegated to a supplementary not provided. Minor editorial issues ('analisys', stray punctuation, brief Prior Work section) suggest the manuscript could be polished further.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: bypassing the decode-encode loop by using undecoded generative latents directly as privileged information is a clean, well-motivated observation, and the Data Processing Inequality framing gives it a plausible theoretical rationale.

MESSy's predictive distillation objective (predicting teacher's modality tokens from the student's visual tokens via lightweight heads, discarded at inference) is a sensible design that avoids rigid embedding matching and adds zero inference cost.

The experimental suite is reasonably thorough for the scale used: teacher efficiency measurements (Table 1), per-modality ablations including isolated synthetic modalities to check for label leakage (Table 2), distillation comparisons against KD and LUGPI baselines (Table 3), NMI alignment analysis (Fig. 3), and qualitative class-level analysis (Fig. 4). Multiple seeds (3 runs) with standard deviations are reported.
The paper is clearly written, with a well-structured three-phase pipeline (Fig. 2) and honest framing of the LUPI/LUGPI lineage.
weaknesses: The information-leakage concern is under-addressed. Both synthetic modalities are deterministic functions of the input image (Hunyuan3D-2 conditions on the image query; audio is generated from Gemma3 captions of the image). So the 'privileged' latents encode image-derived information, not independent physical signals. The isolated-modality check in Table 2 is necessary but not sufficient: a teacher can still exploit image-conditioned generative shortcuts that a visual-only baseline cannot, inflating the apparent value of the 'physical priors' narrative. A stronger control (e.g., latents generated from mismatched or shuffled images) is missing.

The scale of evaluation is a significant limitation for the claims made. All experiments are on Imagenette2-320, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100 with ViT-B/16 for both teacher and student. Given the paper claims a general paradigm shift for synthetic multimodal distillation, at least one large-scale benchmark (e.g., full ImageNet-1k) would be needed to establish credibility; on small benchmarks, memorization and generative-shortcut effects are amplified.

The student-teacher setup is asymmetric only in input modality, not capacity (both ViT-B/16), which weakens the 'capacity interference' argument against L2 matching. Moreover, the central claim that rigid L2 distillation causes 'capacity interference' is asserted with a citation [18] about multimodal optimization, not about distillation geometry; the paper offers no direct evidence isolating this mechanism (e.g., analyzing student feature distortion under L2 vs. MESSy).

The latent-vs-raw teacher comparison (Table 1) is confounded by architecture: the Raw baseline uses a PointNet++ tokenizer and Mel-spectrogram CNN, while the Latent teacher uses Perceiver resamplers on latents. The +7.39% gain cannot be cleanly attributed to the absence of decoding noise versus simply a better fusion architecture for latent inputs. A decoded-latents-then-same-encoder control would be needed.

The DPI-based motivation is loose: it is invoked to argue decoding 'injects noise' reducing I(Y;F), but the downstream classifier is trained on the decoded data, and re-encoding is learnable; the inequality chain as stated does not establish the empirical gains observed. This over-formalizes what is essentially an efficiency-and-regularization argument.

Reproducibility is questionable: key details (latent dimensions, generation hyperparameters, training schedules, cluster construction for NMI) are deferred to a supplementary material that is not included with the submission, and no code release is mentioned. Some claims (e.g., 'full overlap analysis', K ablation) cannot be verified.

Presentation issues suggest limited polish: a stray sentence fragment in Sec. 4 ('...comparisons. . We execute...'), the typo 'analisys' in Sec. 4.2, a sparse two-column Prior Work section, and Table 3's missing 'MM Teacher (UB)' row context in the text discussion. The qualitative analysis (Fig. 4) shows only cherry-picked top classes without reporting the distribution of improvements.

Societal impact and limitations discussion is essentially absent; notably, the risk that generated audio captions could proxy semantic (even class-identifying) information despite name filtering is not analyzed.

strengths: The core idea is original and well-motivated: bypassing the decode-encode loop in LUGPI-style pipelines by using undecoded generative latents (3D and audio codes) directly as privileged information is a clean, sensible contribution with real practical appeal, and the framing via the Data Processing Inequality is intuitive.
The paper is well structured and clearly written, with a coherent three-phase pipeline (synthetic latent generation, multimodal teacher training, predictive distillation) illustrated in Figures 1-2.

The experimental story is unusually complete for this type of work: Table 1 isolates the latent-vs-raw question, Table 2 provides modality ablations including single-synthetic-modality training to rule out label leakage shortcuts, Table 3 compares against KD and LUGPI, and Sections 4.2-4.3 add an emergent-synesthesia NMI analysis and qualitative class-level evidence (Figures 3-4).

Results are consistent across three datasets with standard deviations over 3 independent runs, and MESSy's predictive objective outperforms rigid L2 matching, supporting the capacity-interference hypothesis.
Zero added inference cost is a genuinely valuable property: auxiliary heads are discarded at test time, so the accuracy gains of privileged modalities are retained at unimodal deployment cost.
weaknesses: Scale of evaluation is limited: only Imagenette2-320, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100, with ViT-B/16. It is unclear whether the latent advantage and MESSy gains persist at ImageNet-1k scale or with larger/stronger generative backbones, which weakens the generality claims.

There is a confound in the distillation comparison (Table 3): it is not clearly stated whether the KD and LUGPI baselines distill from the Raw teacher or the stronger Latent teacher. If baselines use the weaker raw pipeline, the reported advantage of MESSy over LUGPI conflates the distillation objective with the teacher quality. An L2-matching baseline on the same latent teacher is needed in the main text (apparently deferred to supplementary).

The student is described as 'lightweight' but uses the same ViT-B/16 architecture as the teacher; the actual capacity difference comes only from removed modality branches, so the capacity-interference argument rests on weaker footing than implied.

The 'capacity interference' claim and the informal DPI argument are plausible but not rigorously established; no direct measurement (e.g., student feature geometry degradation under L2 matching) is provided in the main paper.

Key methodological details are deferred to a supplementary that is not part of the submission (generation prompts, K ablation, VRAM/timing methodology, cluster-overlap analysis), which hurts reproducibility and independent verification of the efficiency claims (87.7% time reduction, VRAM savings).

Some design choices are under-justified: the aggressive modality dropout p=0.8, the choice of K=3 layers, the 100-token Perceiver budget, and the cluster counts used for the NMI analysis are stated without motivation; the NMI cluster evaluation also risks artifacts from overlapping semantics between clusters and class labels.

Presentation polish issues: minor typos ('analisys'), a stray sentence fragment in Section 4, and a somewhat thin related-work section that omits much of the cross-modal distillation and privileged-information literature beyond the cited subset; the predictive cross-modal distillation idea itself has close relatives that deserve comparison.
Societal impact and failure modes of the generative pipeline (e.g., biases or hallucinated physics in synthesized latents propagating into the student) are not discussed.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: the Decode-Encode Loop inefficiency in synthetic multimodal augmentation is a genuine and underexplored observation, and Direct Latent Augmentation (DLA) is a simple, practical remedy with quantified savings (87.7% 3D generation time, 23.8% audio VRAM).

Unusually careful experimental controls for this type of paper: the Raw+Perc. baseline disentangles Perceiver-architecture gains from representation-quality gains (attributing only ~14% of the gap to architecture), modality-combination ablations (Table 2) isolate each modality's contribution, and synthetic-modality-only baselines (Audio-Only 13.07% on ImageNet-100) are used to probe label leakage through the captioning pipeline.

The 'emergent synesthesia' analysis (Sec. 4.4) goes beyond accuracy: NMI alignment between student visual clusters and hand-crafted (semantics-free) audio/3D feature spaces provides genuinely interesting evidence that the distillation objective transfers physical, not merely label-correlated, structure.

MESSy is honestly positioned relative to prior predictor-head methods (BYOL, data2vec, AV-data2vec, JEPA, Zhao et al.), and the target ablation (CLS-Pred vs. auxiliary-modality targets) shows the gains are not purely architectural. The capacity-interference evidence via CIFAR-100 linear probing is a nice mechanism-level validation.
Scalability is verified beyond toy benchmarks with the full ImageNet-1K run, and the student consistently recovers ~68% of the teacher gap, supporting the paper's scaling claims.
Student retains zero inference overhead (heads discarded), so the method is deployment-relevant rather than only a training-time curiosity.
weaknesses: The latent-vs-raw comparison has a residual confound: the raw-teacher encoders (PointNet++-style tokenizer, from-scratch 2D conv on Mel-spectrograms) are trained from scratch on 50 epochs of synthetic data, whereas the latent path implicitly leverages the generative models' massive external pretraining. A fairer control using strong pretrained raw encoders (e.g., EnCodec, CLAP, pretrained audio/3D encoders) is missing, so the DPI-based interpretation of the gap may overstate the 'decoder noise' explanation.

The information-theoretic argument is informal and somewhat overstated: Eq. (1) establishes only an upper-bound ordering, yet the text claims DLA 'theoretically guarantees' higher achievable I(Y;·); a higher bound says nothing about whether the teacher/student optimization can realize it. The empirical claims survive, but the theory section should be softened.

The 'synesthesia' framing risks overclaiming: synthetic audio latents carry strongly class-correlated signal (Audio-Only reaches 54.61% on 10-class Imagenette, 13.07% on 100-class ImageNet-100). While class-correlated privileged information is legitimate under the LUPI paradigm, the narrative that the student internalizes 'physical priors' is only partially supported; the HC-feature NMI results help, but a direct causal demonstration is lacking.

Main results are on small benchmarks (Imagenette2, Caltech101, ImageNet-100) with ViT-B/16; on ImageNet-1K the absolute numbers (teacher 71.32%, student 69.05%) are modest and there is no comparison against strong external distillation baselines (e.g., DeiT-style distillation, CLIP logit distillation) to contextualize whether the multimodal-synthetic pipeline is competitive per unit of compute.

The closest competing objective for capacity interference — a trainable projector as in Zhao et al. [48] — is cited but not empirically compared; comparisons are limited to plain KD and LUGPI's rigid L2.

MESSy's novelty is incremental: predictor heads over multi-layer teacher features are standard; the contribution reduces to the choice of target (pooled auxiliary-modality summaries) and its combination with DLA. This is fine as a component but limits the paper's conceptual weight.

Minor reporting issues: some ablation entries are approximate without standard deviations ('~62.31', '~64.03'), and the claim that augmentation removes the need for paired data should acknowledge the dependence on the quality/bias of frozen off-the-shelf generators (which the conclusion does note as a limitation).

strengths: The core observation is sensible and well-motivated: decoding generative latents into raw signals only to re-encode them in a teacher is wasteful, and bypassing this 'Decode-Encode Loop' is a practical, generalizable idea for LUPI-style training.

The experimental design is more careful than typical for this line of work: the Raw+Perc. control isolates representation quality from resampler architecture, Audio-Only/3D-Only baselines plus a caption-filtering pipeline rule out trivial label leakage, and a CIFAR-100 linear probe on frozen students provides direct evidence for the claimed capacity-interference effect.

Ablations are targeted and informative (CLS-Pred vs. MESSy targets isolates architectural from objective gains; DLA vs. raw teacher per objective), and results are reported over 3 runs with standard deviations.
An ImageNet-1K run validates that the pipeline scales beyond toy benchmarks, with student gap-recovery (~68% of teacher gap) consistent with the smaller-scale results.

The emergent-alignment analysis using both hand-crafted (MFCC, covariance) and deep (CLAP, PointNet) targets is a thoughtful attempt to verify the 'synesthesia' claim beyond accuracy numbers, and the HC-feature alignment is a nontrivial finding.

Clear writing with a well-organized three-phase pipeline, honest limitation statement (frozen off-the-shelf generators), and useful computational-cost quantification (87.7% 3D generation time reduction).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the distillation contribution: the related-work section itself concedes that asymmetric predictor-head distillation is the core of BYOL/data2vec/AV-data2vec/JEPA, and that Zhao et al. independently formalize capacity interference with a projector remedy. MESSy is best read as applying this established pattern to pooled synthetic-modality summaries; the effect sizes over LUGPI (+2.8 to +3.4 pp) are solid but the conceptual delta is incremental.

The audio modality is semantically mediated rather than physical: the audio latent is generated from a Gemma3 caption of the image, so the 'acoustic prior' the student internalizes is largely LLM-derived semantic description of the scene, not low-level acoustic structure of a real signal. This substantially weakens the physical-prior and synesthesia narrative; a comparison against distilling the caption text embeddings directly (skipping audio generation entirely) is needed to show the audio generation step adds anything.

The information-theoretic argument (Sec. 3.1) overreaches: the DPI inequality is trivially true for any deterministic post-processing and does not establish that latent supervision improves downstream accuracy, since the relevant quantity is what a finite-capacity teacher can extract, not the mutual information upper bound. Eq. (3) shows only that conditioning cannot hurt in the idealized infinite-capacity limit. The framing 'theoretically guarantees a higher upper bound' should be softened.

The raw-synthetic baselines use comparatively weak encoders (PointNet++-style tokenizer, Mel-spectrogram 2D CNNs). Raw+Perc. mitigates but does not fully eliminate this concern, and no attempt is made to strengthen the raw encoding path further (e.g., pretrained modality encoders), leaving the magnitude of the latent advantage somewhat uncertain.

Benchmark scope is narrow: three small datasets dominate, and absolute numbers are modest (e.g., 66.5% on Caltech101, 69.05% on ImageNet-1K). Baselines are limited to KD and LUGPI; stronger contrastive distillation (CRD, cited but not compared) and the concurrent capacity-interference remedy of Zhao et al. are absent, making it hard to gauge where MESSy sits in the broader distillation landscape.

Several important details are deferred to supplementary material (K-layer ablation, modality-dropout ablation, prompt/filtering details, VRAM benchmarks), so the main text alone does not fully support the hyperparameter choices.

Heavy branding ('synesthesia', 'pristine latents', 'biomimetic') outruns the evidence at times; the qualitative class-level analysis in Fig. 7 is anecdotal and could be cherry-picked despite being presented as mechanism-level validation.

strengths: The core observation is interesting and well-motivated: bypassing the decode-encode loop of generative augmentation by consuming undecoded latents (DLA) is a simple but under-explored idea, and the information-theoretic framing (Data Processing Inequality, chain rule of mutual information) gives an intuitive justification.

Experimental controls are unusually thorough for this type of paper. The Raw+Perc. baseline isolates the Perceiver resampler architecture from the representation-quality claim (attributing ~14% of the gap to architecture, the rest to the undecoded latents). Modality-only baselines (Audio-Only 13%, 3D-Only 39%) plausibly rule out trivial label leakage, and the CLS-Pred ablation separates the effect of the projection heads from the effect of the prediction target.

The capacity-interference claim is supported with an appropriately designed out-of-task probe (CIFAR-100 linear evaluation of frozen ImageNet-100 students), which is a clean way to show L2 matching degrades visual discriminability while MESSy preserves it.

The emergent-synesthesia analysis (NMI against hand-crafted vs. deep audio/3D feature spaces) goes beyond accuracy numbers and provides mechanistic evidence that the student's visual space aligns with unobserved physical statistics, not just label co-occurrence.

Scalability is verified beyond toy settings with a full ImageNet-1K run, and the student consistently recovers ~68% of the teacher gap across scales; results are averaged over 3 runs with standard deviations.

Related work is honest and precise about the relationship to AV-data2vec, JEPA, CRD, and Zhao et al.'s capacity-interference formalization, clearly delineating MESSy's distinction (predicting pooled auxiliary-modality summaries rather than self-features or teacher CLS tokens).
weaknesses: The novelty of MESSy is modest. Asymmetric predictor heads that predict frozen teacher representations are the standard BYOL/data2vec recipe, and Zhao et al. [48] already formalized the capacity-interference problem with a trainable projector as the remedy. The paper's claim of distinctness rests mainly on the choice of target (auxiliary-modality summaries), which is a reasonable but incremental delta; this should be stated more plainly.

The theoretical argument is informal and slightly overclaimed. The DPI (Eq. 1) only establishes that decoding cannot increase mutual information; it does not 'theoretically guarantee a higher upper bound on I' in any operational sense, since the realized information depends entirely on the learned encoders. The SNR/noisy-channel narrative is plausible but heuristic.

The raw-data baseline comparison may partially favor the proposed method: the raw teachers use from-scratch PointNet++ and Mel-spectrogram 2D-conv encoders, which are known to be weak without large-scale pretraining, whereas the latent teacher consumes representations from heavily pretrained generative models. The Raw+Perc. control helps, but the comparison conflates representation quality with the benefit of foundation-model pretraining.

Generality is limited: all experiments use ViT-B/16, a single teacher/student architecture pair, and a specific frozen generator stack (Hunyuan3D-2, Gemma3, AudioGen). No experiments probe sensitivity to backbone scale, alternative generators, or dense/other downstream tasks; conclusions about the framework's generality therefore rest on one configuration per dataset.

Some reported numbers are imprecise: Table 4 (right) uses '~62.31' and '~64.03' rather than mean ± std across runs, unlike every other table, weakening an ablation that is central to the DLA-isolation claim.

The audio pipeline carries a residual leakage risk that is mitigated but not fully eliminable: the LLM caption is generated from the image itself, so the 'audio' signal is fundamentally derived from visual content, and the Audio-Only accuracy (13% vs. 1% chance) confirms class-relevant signal flows through the caption path. The WordNet-synonym filtering is a good faith effort, but a stronger control (e.g., captions generated from a held-out modality or from text-only descriptors) would be more convincing.

The emergent-synesthesia NMI analysis depends on clustering hyperparameters (cluster counts, algorithm) that are deferred to supplementary material; sensitivity of the reported alignment gains to these choices is not established in the main text.

No code or data release is mentioned in the main text, which for a paper whose pipeline spans four large pretrained models (Hunyuan3D, Gemma3, AudioGen, ViT) and requires generating latents for 1.28M images raises reproducibility concerns.
